qa-1: We'd like to hear how you would put together the overall testing approach for a product team that is just starting out: what you would decide, write down and agree with the team, and how you would go about it.
qa-2: Imagine a release is due in three days and four in ten of your regression tests have not yet been run. Talk us through, step by step, how you would handle the situation and the decisions involved.
qa-3: Shift-left means bringing testing earlier in development; shift-right means testing and learning from production. Explain both ideas and give examples of practices you have actually put in place yourself.
qa-4: The test pyramid, testing trophy and test honeycomb are different models for balancing unit, integration and end-to-end tests. Compare them and tell us which kinds of system or situation each one suits.
qa-5: When a product owner (PO) writes acceptance criteria for a story, how do you work with them so the criteria are clear and precise enough to test against? Describe what you actually do in practice.
qa-6: Ten microservice teams ship together on a single scheduled release cadence, known as a release train. Design how you would organise quality across them, talking through your reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
qa-7: Exploratory testing is unscripted testing where the tester learns and designs tests as they go. How do you organise that work so it stays focused, and how do you report what came out of it?
qa-8: If you were starting a new web application project, how would you choose between the Playwright, Cypress and Selenium browser automation tools? Compare their strengths and weaknesses and explain how you would reach a decision.
qa-9: Explain what auto-waiting and web-first assertions are in browser test tools, and how they help reduce flaky tests, meaning tests that pass or fail inconsistently without any change to the code.
qa-10: Locators are how automated UI tests find elements on a page. Tell us how you decide which kind of locator to use, and why, so that tests stay reliable as the interface changes.
qa-11: Design an automated UI test framework that will still be fast, reliable and maintainable when it grows to around two thousand tests. Talk through its structure, your reasoning and the trade-offs; there is no single right answer.
qa-12: Most end-to-end (E2E) tests need a signed-in user, and logging in through the UI every time is slow. How do you handle authentication in your E2E suites so it is quick, reliable and secure?
qa-13: In browser or API tests you can either fake the backend's network responses or call the real services. How do you decide which to do, and how do you balance the two across a suite?
qa-14: Visual regression testing compares screenshots to catch unintended changes in how the UI looks. Describe how you would set it up and the practical problems you have seen, or would expect, with it.
qa-15: For a React application, how do you decide what to cover with component tests, which render pieces of the UI in isolation, versus end-to-end tests that drive the whole app in a real browser?
qa-16: Playwright now offers AI agents that plan tests, generate test code and heal broken tests. How would you assess whether tools like these are worth adopting in your team, and what would you weigh up?
qa-17: You cannot test on every browser, operating system and device. How do you decide which ones your testing should cover, and how would you justify that choice to the team?
qa-18: Beyond checking that a REST API works with valid input, what else do you test? Walk us through the kinds of tests you would add to cover the less obvious behaviour and the failure cases.
qa-19: Consumer-driven contract testing checks that services agree on the requests and responses they exchange. Explain how it works in practice and the situations where you would decide it is not worth the effort.
qa-20: GraphQL is a query language where clients ask a single endpoint for exactly the data they need. How does your approach to testing a GraphQL API differ from the way you test a REST API?
qa-21: Your API tests pass on your own machine but sometimes fail in the continuous integration (CI) pipeline with HTTP 401 errors. Walk us through, step by step, how you would track down the cause.
qa-22: Some systems process work asynchronously, passing messages through queues rather than responding straight away. How do you write reliable tests for flows like that, where the outcome only appears some time later?
qa-23: Apigee is Google's API management gateway and Akamai is a content delivery network and edge security platform. When the APIs you test sit behind these layers, what changes about how you test them?
qa-24: Explain the difference between load, stress, soak and spike testing: what each of these kinds of performance test is designed to tell you, and when you would run it.
qa-25: A new checkout is launching and must cope with five times today's traffic. Design the performance testing you would do beforehand, talking through your reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
qa-26: After a release, the 99th-percentile response time (the slowest one per cent of requests) doubled while the median stayed the same. Walk us through, step by step, how you would investigate.
qa-27: These are two load-testing concepts about how test tools generate traffic and measure response times. Explain what each term means and why it matters when deciding whether to trust a performance test's results.
qa-28: How do you test the performance of a website as the user experiences it in their browser, rather than just server response times? Describe the techniques and measures you would use.
qa-29: Describe how tests are spread across the stages of a delivery pipeline, from a code change to production, and what each stage should be allowed to stop or approve before work moves on.
qa-30: About fifteen per cent of your end-to-end test runs fail at random with no code change. Tell us, step by step, how you would tackle this and make the suite trustworthy again.
qa-31: To speed up large test suites you can run tests in parallel or split them across machines, known as sharding. How do you do that without tests interfering with each other or giving misleading results?
qa-32: Ephemeral preview environments are short-lived copies of the application created for a particular change. How have you used them, or how would you, and what do you need to get right for them to work well?
qa-33: Which automated checks do you think should be able to stop a code change from being merged, and which should not? Explain the reasoning behind your choices.
qa-34: Test impact analysis means running only the tests affected by a given code change. Explain how it works and what could go wrong if a team relies on it.
qa-35: Tell us how you manage test data: where it comes from, how each test gets the data it needs, and how you keep it reliable across environments and repeated runs.
qa-36: A test environment you share with other teams keeps breaking because of their changes, and it is blocking your testing. Talk us through, step by step, what you would do, both straight away and longer term.
qa-37: Stubs, mocks, fakes and service virtualisation are all ways of standing in for real dependencies during testing. Explain what each one is, how they differ, and when you would use each.
qa-38: Accessibility means making sure people with disabilities, including those using assistive technology, can use the product. Describe how you test for it and how that fits into the team's normal way of working.
qa-39: Thinking about the split between testers and dedicated security specialists, which kinds of security testing do you believe a QA engineer or QA team should own, and why?
qa-40: Feature flags let teams switch functionality on or off without redeploying, and configuration settings change behaviour in a similar way. How do you test software whose behaviour depends on flags and configuration?
qa-41: Resilience or chaos testing deliberately introduces failures to see how a system copes. What role should QA play in that work, and what would you personally contribute to it?
qa-42: Which measures of quality do you report to teams and leadership, and which commonly used ones do you deliberately avoid? Explain your reasoning for each.
qa-43: Senior leaders ask why bugs still reach production when the team has two thousand automated tests. How would you answer them, and what would you do afterwards? Take us through your approach.
qa-44: Describe what a good bug report contains, and how you run triage, the regular process of reviewing newly reported bugs and deciding what happens to each of them.
qa-45: Tell us about one particular time you changed how a team approached quality. We want the real story: what you yourself did to bring the change about, and how it turned out.
qa-46: Describe a real occasion when you disagreed with a product manager or development lead about whether a release was ready to go out. What did you personally do, and what happened in the end?
qa-47: Give us a concrete example of mentoring a tester, or of helping developers get better at testing. Tell us who it was, what you yourself did, and what changed for them as a result.
qa-48: Tell us about a defect that reached production which you, or your testing, should have caught. Walk us through what happened, what you did about it, and what you took from it.
qa-49: Tell us about a specific time you brought a new testing tool or framework into a team. Explain why, what you personally did to introduce it, and how it worked out.
qa-50: Describe a real time when capacity was tight and you had to decide how much effort went into automation versus manual testing. How did you decide, what did you do, and what was the outcome?
web-1: The event loop is how JavaScript schedules work on a single thread. Explain how it works and the difference between microtasks and macrotasks, including what that means for code running in the browser.
web-2: In a single-page application (SPA) that stays open for hours, closures can keep memory alive longer than intended. Explain how that happens and how you would find and fix such a leak.
web-3: We'd like your honest view of TypeScript: where its type system genuinely protects you, and where it can give a false sense of safety. Concrete examples from your own code are welcome.
web-4: In asynchronous JavaScript, how do you deal with errors, and with cancelling work that is no longer needed, such as a request for a page the user has already left? Describe the patterns you use.
web-5: Tree-shaking is when a bundler removes code your application never uses. Explain what makes a module or library easy or hard to tree-shake, and how you write code with that in mind.
web-6: Web Workers run JavaScript on a background thread rather than the browser's main thread. When would you move work into a worker, when would you not, and what costs come with doing so?
web-7: Explain how React works out what to update on the page when state changes, known as reconciliation, and what typically makes components re-render when they do not need to. How would you spot and fix that?
web-8: Compare React Server Components with server-side rendering (SSR), client-side rendering (CSR) and static site generation (SSG). How do you decide which approach to use for a given page or application?
web-9: How do you decide where state should live in a frontend application, and which tools to use for managing it? Talk us through your reasoning with examples.
web-10: Eight product teams need a shared library of UI components. Design how you would build and run it, talking us through your reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
web-11: Micro-frontends split one web frontend into parts that separate teams build and deploy independently. When do you think that approach pays off, and when does it cost more than it gives?
web-12: What do you do to make web forms reliable and pleasant to use, from the moment a user starts typing through to submission? Describe the approach and techniques you rely on.
web-13: Users report that a React page freezes or lags while they type into a search box. Walk us through, step by step, how you would find the cause and what you might do about it.
web-14: Describe, in as much depth as you can, what happens between a user typing a web address into the browser and the first content being drawn on the screen.
web-15: Core Web Vitals are Google's set of metrics for real-world page experience. Explain what each one measures and how you would go about improving each of them.
web-16: Explain how browsers and other caches decide whether they can reuse a stored copy of a resource, and the HTTP response headers you use to control that behaviour.
web-17: How do you make sure the web applications you build can be used by people with disabilities? Describe what you do during design, development and testing.
web-18: CORS, or Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, controls when a web page may call a server on a different origin. Explain how it works, what a preflight request is, and when the browser sends one.
web-19: CSP, or Content Security Policy, is an HTTP header that restricts what a page is allowed to load and run. Explain what it protects against and how you would introduce it on an existing site.
web-20: In your view, what separates a well-designed REST API from a poor one? Tell us the qualities and conventions you look for when designing or reviewing one.
web-21: Compare REST, GraphQL and gRPC as styles for building APIs. When would you choose each one, and what are you trading off when you do?
web-22: An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. How do you design write operations, such as placing an order, so that clients and systems can safely retry them?
web-23: Design a public API that limits how many requests each client can make. Talk through your design aloud, including the reasoning and trade-offs; there is no single right answer.
web-24: When one service needs another, it can either call it synchronously and wait for a reply, or communicate asynchronously. How do you choose between the two, and what are the consequences of each?
web-25: When your service calls other services or databases, how do you set up timeouts and retries, and what else do you do to stop a slow or failing dependency from causing wider problems?
web-26: How do you change an API over time, adding and altering features, without breaking the clients that already depend on it? Describe the practices you follow.
web-27: You are building a new service and need to choose between a relational SQL database and a NoSQL one. How would you make that decision, and what would you take into account?
web-28: A database query that used to be fast has become slow as the amount of data grew. Walk us through, step by step, how you would investigate and fix it.
web-29: Database isolation levels control how concurrent transactions see each other's changes. Explain the main levels and illustrate them with a concrete problem you have seen, or could see, when two transactions overlap.
web-30: Talk us through the caching strategies you use in web applications, and how you keep cached data correct when the underlying data changes.
web-31: How do you change a database schema on a live system without taking the application offline? Explain the approach you would take for a change such as renaming or splitting a column.
web-32: OAuth 2.0's authorisation code flow with PKCE, Proof Key for Code Exchange, is the usual way apps obtain access tokens. Walk us through how the flow works and where OpenID Connect (OIDC) fits on top.
web-33: In a single-page application (SPA) running in the browser, where should access and refresh tokens be kept? Explain the options and the security trade-offs between them.
web-34: A JWT, or JSON Web Token, is a signed token often used for authentication. Explain everything your server should check before it trusts a JWT it has received.
web-35: The OWASP Top 10 is a widely used list of the most critical web application security risks, and it was updated for 2025. Tell us what changed in that edition and how you defend against those risks.
web-36: In a multi-tenant application, many customer organisations share the same system. How do you make sure each user can only see and change what they are allowed to, especially other tenants' data?
web-37: How do you handle secrets such as passwords and API keys, and the third-party packages your code depends on, so that neither becomes a security weakness in your applications?
web-38: Design a service that lets people across a large company store and share documents. Talk through your design aloud, including the reasoning and trade-offs; there is no single right answer.
web-39: Design a system that delivers real-time notifications to around a hundred thousand users connected at the same time. Talk us through your reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
web-40: Design a way for users of a web application to upload files as large as five gigabytes. Talk through your design, reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
web-41: Design a service for managing feature flags, which let teams switch functionality on or off without redeploying. Talk through your design, reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
web-42: As a senior engineer, how do you approach testing the code you and your team write? Tell us what kinds of tests you write and how you decide what is worth testing.
web-43: What does a good continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) set-up look like for a web application? Describe the path a change takes from commit to production.
web-44: Users intermittently get HTTP 502 Bad Gateway errors, but your application logs show nothing. Talk us through, step by step, how you would work out what is going on.
web-45: Code review is when teammates check each other's changes before they are merged. Using a real example, tell us how you give feedback as a reviewer and how you take it as an author.
web-46: Tell us about one particular technical decision you pushed for even though others disagreed. Describe what you yourself did, how the disagreement was handled, and what happened.
web-47: Describe a real time you helped a colleague grow to the next level in their career, for example from mid-level to senior. What did you personally do, and how did it go?
web-48: Think of one production incident that you led or helped resolve. Talk us through what happened, the part you yourself played, and what came of it afterwards.
web-49: Tell us about a real occasion when you had to weigh paying down technical debt against delivering new features. How did you approach it, what did you do, and what was the outcome?
web-50: Tell us about a project you were part of that failed or slipped badly. We want to hear what happened, what your own role was, and what you would do differently now.
edge-1: Akamai is a content delivery network, or CDN. Walk us through the path a user's request takes from their browser, through Akamai's platform, to the origin server and back again.
edge-2: In Akamai Property Manager, the tool for configuring delivery, you can set cache lifetimes, known as TTLs. Explain how those settings combine with the caching headers the origin server sends, and how the two interact in practice.
edge-3: A cache key is what a CDN uses to decide whether two requests are for the same cached object. Explain what makes up a cache key and how you would change it without causing problems.
edge-4: After a new release, users still see old versions of pages or files served through Akamai. Walk us through, step by step, how you would confirm the cause and fix it.
edge-5: Purging removes or refreshes content held in Akamai's caches. What different ways of purging are available, and how do you decide which one to use in a given situation?
edge-6: In Akamai Property Manager, a property is a delivery configuration. Explain how its versions work, how a version is activated, and how rules inherit settings from the rules above them.
edge-7: Without access to Akamai's own servers, how do you investigate what Akamai did with a request and why a response looks the way it does? Describe the tools and techniques you use.
edge-8: EdgeWorkers is Akamai's service for running your own code on its edge servers. When is it a good choice, and when would you avoid it?
edge-9: How do you set up Akamai so traffic can be spread across several origin servers or data centres, and moved away from one that fails? Explain the options and how you would choose between them.
edge-10: Design Akamai delivery for an application running in several regions that also exposes APIs, where different content needs different caching. Talk through your reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
edge-11: App & API Protector is Akamai's web application and API security product. Describe what protection it provides and how you tune it so it stops attacks without disrupting legitimate users.
edge-12: Login and search endpoints are common targets for abuse. How would you set up Akamai rate controls, which limit how often clients can make requests, to protect those endpoints?
edge-13: Akamai offers basic bot visibility and a fuller Bot Manager product for dealing with automated traffic. Explain the difference between them and when the full product is worth having.
edge-14: DDoS means distributed denial-of-service, an attack that floods a service with traffic. Explain how you would protect a site against it at each layer, from the network up to the application.
edge-15: Locking down an origin means stopping attackers from bypassing Akamai and reaching your servers directly. Explain what Akamai's Site Shield does and what other ways exist to protect the origin.
edge-16: CPS is Akamai's Certificate Provisioning System for TLS certificates, and mTLS is mutual TLS, where both sides present certificates. Explain how you manage certificates on Akamai and where mTLS comes in.
edge-17: Rather than changing Akamai configuration by hand in the web console, how do you manage it as code? Describe the tools and the workflow you would use.
edge-18: Design a continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) process for making Akamai configuration changes safely. Talk through the steps, your reasoning and the trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
edge-19: DataStream streams Akamai's delivery logs and mPulse measures real users' experience. What do you use these, and Akamai's other logs, for, and how do you get value from them?
edge-20: Just after you activate a new Akamai configuration, about thirty per cent of requests start getting 503 errors from the origin. Talk us through, step by step, what you would do.
edge-21: CP codes, short for content provider codes, are identifiers Akamai attaches to traffic. Explain how you use them for reporting, and for charging costs back to the right teams.
edge-22: Apigee is Google's API management platform. Describe how an Apigee API proxy is put together: its main parts, and how a request and its response move through it.
edge-23: Apigee X is the Google Cloud-hosted version of Apigee. Explain what organisations, environments, environment groups and instances are, and how they relate to each other.
edge-24: In Apigee, shared flows are reusable pieces of proxy logic and flow hooks attach them automatically. Explain how you would use these to apply consistent standards across many API proxies.
edge-25: In Apigee, a target server is a named definition of a backend that proxies call. Explain why you would use target servers rather than writing backend addresses directly into each proxy.
edge-26: Apigee offers key value maps (KVMs) and property sets for holding data a proxy needs at runtime. What kind of information belongs in each, and what should not go in either?
edge-27: Explain how API products, developer apps and API keys work together in Apigee to control which consumers can use which APIs.
edge-28: Quota, SpikeArrest and ConcurrentRateLimit are Apigee policies that limit traffic. Explain how they differ from one another and when you would use each.
edge-29: How do you make sure that, when something goes wrong in an Apigee proxy, clients receive errors in a consistent and safe way? Describe how you would set that up.
edge-30: Apigee lets you add custom logic with JavaScript or Java callouts, and call other services with the ServiceCallout policy. When do you reach for these, and what limits or downsides do they have?
edge-31: A proxy in Apigee X is not behaving as expected. Describe the tools and steps you would use to find out what is happening to requests as they pass through it.
edge-32: In Apigee X, northbound means traffic from clients into Apigee and southbound means traffic from Apigee to backends. Describe the networking options for each direction and how you would choose.
edge-33: The OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant lets one application get a token to call an API as itself, with no user involved. Explain how you would implement it with Apigee.
edge-34: Compare API keys, OAuth tokens, JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) and mutual TLS (mTLS) as ways of securing APIs. How do they differ, and when would you use which?
edge-35: Apigee has threat-protection policies and a separate add-on called Advanced API Security. Explain what each one does and how you would use them to protect your APIs.
edge-36: A partner says they are getting HTTP 429 Too Many Requests errors from your API even though they are staying within their agreed limits. Walk us through, step by step, how you would investigate.
edge-37: Sensitive data such as personal details or credentials can leak out through an API gateway. How would you stop that happening with Apigee? Tell us where the risks lie and what you would do.
edge-38: Design a continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) pipeline for building, testing and deploying Apigee API proxies. Talk through the stages, reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
edge-39: How do you use Apigee's analytics and monitoring features to understand how your APIs are performing and to spot problems early? Describe what you would set up and watch.
edge-40: Apigee comes as the Google-hosted Apigee X or as Apigee hybrid, where you operate part of the platform yourself. Explain how they differ and the circumstances in which you would choose hybrid.
edge-41: API hub is Google's catalogue for keeping track of an organisation's APIs. Explain how you would use it to support API governance, meaning consistent standards and oversight across teams.
edge-42: Design an architecture where traffic passes through Akamai, then Apigee X, to backend services hosted on both Google Cloud and Azure. Talk it through aloud with your reasoning and trade-offs; there is no single right answer.
edge-43: Thirty teams build APIs across the organisation. Design the standards and processes you would put in place so their APIs are consistent and secure, talking through your reasoning aloud; there is no single right answer.
edge-44: API response times are spiking and both the Akamai and Apigee monitoring dashboards are showing red. You are leading the response: walk us through, step by step, what you would do.
edge-45: Tell us about a real change you made to a shared platform that affected many teams. How did you carry it out, what did you personally do, and how did it go?
edge-46: Describe one particular time a team asked your platform team for something and you said no. How did you handle it, and what happened afterwards?
edge-47: Tell us about a real security incident, or a near miss, involving your edge network or API gateway. Talk us through what happened, what you yourself did, and what changed afterwards.
edge-48: Toil is repetitive manual operational work that adds no lasting value. Tell us about a specific time you cut it down for your platform team, what you did, and the difference it made.
edge-49: Describe a real occasion when you had to escalate a problem to a vendor such as Akamai or Google. Tell us what the problem was, how you handled the escalation, and how it ended.
edge-50: Tell us about a time you helped other engineers build their skills with the platforms you look after. What did you personally do, and what difference did it make?
aks-1: Walk us through, in as much detail as you can, everything that happens inside a Kubernetes cluster between running kubectl apply on a Deployment manifest and the application's pods running.
aks-2: In Kubernetes, containers can declare resource requests and limits for CPU and memory, and each pod gets a Quality of Service (QoS) class. Explain what these mean and how they affect a pod's behaviour.
aks-3: Kubernetes has liveness, readiness and startup probes for checking a container's health. Explain what each one is for and the common ways teams misuse them.
aks-4: A PDB, or PodDisruptionBudget, limits how many of an application's pods can be taken down at once. Explain how PDBs interact with cluster upgrades and with autoscaling, and what can go wrong.
aks-5: What tools does Kubernetes give you to influence which nodes pods run on and how they are spread out? Explain how and when you would use each of them.
aks-6: Explain how Kubernetes Services route traffic to pods, the role played by kube-proxy or eBPF-based alternatives, and how DNS name resolution works inside a cluster.
aks-7: A Kubernetes controller, sometimes called an operator, is software that watches resources and acts to bring the cluster to a desired state. How would you build and run one safely in production?
aks-8: AKS is Azure Kubernetes Service, Microsoft's managed Kubernetes offering. Describe how an AKS cluster is put together and which parts Microsoft looks after versus which parts are your responsibility.
aks-9: A node pool is a group of identically configured virtual machines in an AKS cluster. How do you decide how many node pools to have and how to configure each of them?
aks-10: AKS clusters can be created in two modes, Automatic and Standard. Explain how the two differ and how you would decide which to use for a given cluster.
aks-11: AKS offers several CNI (Container Network Interface) models for giving pods IP addresses: Azure CNI Overlay, Pod Subnet, the legacy Node Subnet, and kubenet. Compare them and say when each fits.
aks-12: Azure CNI Powered by Cilium is an AKS networking option built on the open-source Cilium project. Explain what it gives you compared with the other AKS networking options.
aks-13: The community ingress-nginx controller, widely used to route external HTTP traffic into clusters, was retired in March 2026. Tell us how you would plan ingress for AKS from here and move existing workloads across.
aks-14: Gateway API is the newer Kubernetes standard for routing traffic into a cluster. Describe its main resource types and explain why it matters compared with the older Ingress resource.
aks-15: Design an AKS cluster whose API server is not exposed to the internet and whose outbound traffic is tightly controlled. Talk through your reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
aks-16: Pods in your AKS cluster cannot connect to an Azure SQL database that is reachable only through a private endpoint. Walk us through, step by step, how you would troubleshoot it.
aks-17: Microsoft Entra Workload ID lets pods on AKS authenticate to Azure services as an Azure identity. Explain how it works end to end, from the pod to it receiving a usable Azure token.
aks-18: People need access to AKS clusters. Compare using Azure role-based access control (RBAC) with native Kubernetes RBAC to decide who can do what, and describe how you would set up cluster access.
aks-19: AKS relies on several Azure managed identities to do its work. Which identities are involved, what is each one used for, and how should their permissions be set?
aks-20: ACR is Azure Container Registry. How do you make sure your AKS clusters pull container images from it securely? Describe the set-up you would put in place and why.
aks-21: Azure Policy can enforce rules about what is deployed to AKS clusters. Explain how it works with AKS and what baseline set of rules you would apply.
aks-22: Pod Security Standards are Kubernetes' predefined security profiles for pods. How would you enforce them across an AKS cluster, and what kinds of setting do they cover?
aks-23: When several teams share a cluster, each in its own namespace, how do you use Kubernetes network policies to control traffic between their workloads?
aks-24: How do you handle secrets such as passwords, keys and certificates for applications running on AKS? Describe the options available and what you would recommend.
aks-25: Microsoft Defender for Containers is Azure's security product for container environments. What does it add on top of an AKS cluster's built-in security, and how would you use it?
aks-26: HPA is the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, VPA the Vertical Pod Autoscaler, and KEDA is Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling. Explain what each does and when you would use them, alone or together.
aks-27: Cluster Autoscaler and Node Auto Provisioning, which is based on the open-source Karpenter project, both add and remove nodes in AKS. Compare how they work and when you would choose each.
aks-28: During a traffic spike, new pods stay in the Pending state instead of starting. Walk us through, step by step, how you would find out why and get them running.
aks-29: Right-sizing means setting each workload's CPU and memory to what it actually needs. How do you work out the right values, and how do you keep them right over time?
aks-30: Talk us through how you keep AKS clusters up to date, both the Kubernetes version and the nodes themselves, and how you make upgrades safe and predictable.
aks-31: You run around forty AKS clusters spread across several environments. Design how you would upgrade them all safely, talking through your reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
aks-32: An AKS cluster upgrade has stalled because a node will not finish draining, meaning its pods cannot all be moved off. Walk us through, step by step, what you would check.
aks-33: Flux and Argo CD are the two main GitOps tools, which keep a cluster in sync with configuration stored in Git. Compare them for use on AKS and explain how you would choose.
aks-34: Terraform and Bicep are both infrastructure-as-code tools for creating Azure resources. Compare them for building and managing AKS clusters, and explain which you would choose and why.
aks-35: Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes, using charts to template manifests. What practices do you follow when a platform team provides Helm charts for many other teams to use?
aks-36: What would a good observability set-up, covering metrics, logs and traces, look like for AKS clusters and the applications on them? Describe the components and how they fit together.
aks-37: How do you keep AKS costs under control, and how do you work out which teams or applications are responsible for which costs?
aks-38: Monitoring shows AKS node memory close to one hundred per cent, yet no containers are being killed for running out of memory. Walk us through, step by step, how you would interpret that.
aks-39: A critical workload on AKS must keep running even if an entire Azure region fails. Design how you would achieve that, talking through your reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
aks-40: How would you back up an AKS cluster and the applications on it, and how would you restore them after data loss or a disaster? Describe your approach and the tools you would use.
aks-41: A pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff, meaning its container keeps starting, crashing and being restarted. Walk us through, step by step, how you would find out why.
aks-42: Nodes in an AKS cluster keep dropping into the NotReady state now and then before recovering. Talk us through, step by step, how you would investigate the cause.
aks-43: Response times have gone up, but only for traffic travelling between Azure availability zones. Walk us through what could cause that and how you would investigate, step by step.
aks-44: It is two in the morning, you are in the middle of an incident, and an admission policy is rejecting a deployment you need to ship. Talk us through, step by step, what you would do.
aks-45: Design a self-service developer platform on AKS for fifty application teams: what it offers and how teams use it. Talk through your reasoning and trade-offs aloud; there is no single right answer.
aks-46: Tell us about a real incident on a Kubernetes platform that you led. Walk us through what happened, what you yourself did during and after it, and how it ended.
aks-47: Describe one migration you led, for example of ingress, container networking (CNI) or identity. How did you run it, what was your personal role, and how did it turn out?
aks-48: Tell us about one particular time teams pushed back on a standard you wanted them to adopt. What did you do to bring them round, and what was the outcome?
aks-49: Describe a real infrastructure mistake you made that cost money, time or service. Tell us what happened, what you did about it, and what you learned.
